skills.name: Cloudflare
skills.description: Build, deploy and operate real software on Cloudflare — Workers, D1, R2, KV, DNS and domains, Pages, Turnstile and Queues, through the REST API. The capability every Cloudflare-built site or app depends on.

changelog.notes: Credentials move to the gateway secret store: bare names (no USR_ prefix) and a per-key contract (kind, hosts, words) under metadata.orchestra.secrets.

changelog.summary: Deploy from the project folder, not from /tmp — the deploy command reads orchestra/sites/$NAME/worker.js; the record is deploy.json exactly.
Where the project lives: one folder per site under orchestra/sites/<name>/ with worker, schema, DESIGN.md, README and a deploy.json that is treated as a secret.

Fixes a false alarm in the language check. It stripped HTML tags but not the contents of script and style, so a site whose own JavaScript mentioned "comments" or "home" was reported as showing English to readers of another language. The check is about what a reader sees, so it now looks only at that.

Stops warning about a deliberately portable font stack. Shipping no webfont is only a problem when the stack names a face that is not on every platform; the best-looking page to come out of this stack so far is set in Arial and takes its character from scale, weight and colour instead.

Four checks for sites that work but are wrong. Nothing may overlap anything else. The typeface has to reach the reader — a stack led by a macOS-only face with no webfont is a different design on every other machine. The interface has to speak the site’s own language, not show English labels and US dates on a Catalan blog. And a title must not say the same thing twice. All four were found on a live site that passed every existing check.

Catches markup that has become words on the page. A favicon data URI carrying a raw <svg> inside its href closed its own <link> tag early, and a stray glyph and quote-bracket rendered on every route of a live site — while the page answered 200, had a title, and had a favicon link, so every structural check passed. The verifier now reads what the browser actually shows.

Adds a check for the palette every generated site lands on. The verifier now reads the colours the page is actually painted in and warns when they are the default cream-and-terracotta (or near-black-and-acid-green) that arrives regardless of subject — the same palette came out of this stack for a carpentry studio and a municipal swimming pool.

Two fixes from watching an agent use it. The verifier crashed outright when one viewport came back without measurements, throwing away every check that had already passed; a failed measurement is now a warning and the rest of the run continues. And the skill now says a failing check is not advice — the agent ran the checks, read the failure, fixed the two easy ones and reported the site as ready anyway.

The link check now asks what a link actually serves. A site shipped with a "See all" link pointing at its own JSON endpoint: it answered 200, so checking the status alone passed it, and a visitor clicking it got raw JSON in the browser. A link in a page is a promise of a page.

The verifier is now part of what "done" means. It shipped in 0.2.0 but was only mentioned in a reference file, so an agent asked to check a site reached for its own browser instead, looked at the page, and missed a missing favicon and a headline sitting outside the column. The skill now says a deploy is not finished until the checks have run and the screenshots have been opened.

Screenshots no longer land inside the skill. The obvious place to run the verifier from is the folder it lives in, which wrote its output into managed files and left the next update unable to complete. They now go to the Orchestra workspace instead.

Fixes a false alarm in the layout check. It compared the boxes of top-level sections, so any page with a full-bleed header or footer was reported as misaligned — and the correctly-built sections were the ones it named. It now compares where the text starts, which is the question a reader actually asks.

The agent can now look at what it deployed. Adds a verifier it runs after every deploy — it renders the site in a real browser and checks the layout holds, the favicon loads, no API token is being served, and no internal link is broken.
First release. Workers, D1, R2, KV, DNS and domains, Pages, Turnstile and Queues through the REST API.

where.en: console.x.com → your app → Keys & Tokens → OAuth 1.0 Keys → Consumer Key (older guides call it API Key). It is shown once; if you lost it, regenerate it.
where.es: console.x.com → tu app → Keys & Tokens → OAuth 1.0 Keys → Consumer Key (en guías viejas, API Key). Se muestra una sola vez; si la perdiste, regénerala.

X_API_KEY.why: X signs every request with OAuth 1.0a, an HMAC keyed by the two secrets over a text that includes the key and the token. The egress proxy can swap a sentinel into a header but cannot re-sign, so all four keys stay plain variables.

where.es: console.x.com → tu app → Keys & Tokens → OAuth 1.0 Keys → Consumer Secret, junto al Consumer Key (en guías viejas, API Key Secret).

where.en: console.x.com → your app → Keys & Tokens → OAuth 1.0 Keys → Access Token → Generate. First set User authentication settings → App permissions to 'Read and write': a token generated before that stays read-only.
where.es: console.x.com → tu app → Keys & Tokens → OAuth 1.0 Keys → Access Token → Generate. Antes pon User authentication settings → App permissions en 'Read and write': un token generado antes queda de solo lectura.

X_ACCESS_TOKEN.why: X signs every request with OAuth 1.0a, an HMAC keyed by the two secrets over a text that includes the key and the token. The egress proxy can swap a sentinel into a header but cannot re-sign, so all four keys stay plain variables.

skills.name: Month-End Close

Use when the user says "close the month", "month end", "monthly numbers", "P&L for September", "what do I send my accountant", "cash position", "how did we do this month". Not for single invoices (invoice-capture) or categorising one export (expense-categorize).

skills.name: Inbox Triage
skills.description: Go through the person's Gmail inbox and sort it: what needs them today, what can wait, what is waiting on someone else, what is noise — with a one-line summary of each that matters, replies drafted for their yes, and commitments pulled out to track. Never sends, archives or deletes without the rule or the yes. Use when the user says "go through my inbox", "what needs me", "triage my email", "summarise my emails", "draft replies", "inbox zero", "what did I miss". Needs Gmail connected. Not for customer support queues (support-reply).

skills.name: Calendar Management
skills.description: Keep the person's Google Calendar working for them — the day and week ahead with what each meeting needs, conflicts and double bookings found, slots proposed for a meeting request, focus time protected by their rules, and events created or moved only with their yes. Use when the user says "what's my day", "my week", "find a time", "schedule a meeting with", "move my 3pm", "am I free", "block time for", "prep me for my meetings". Needs Google Calendar connected. Not for writing up a meeting afterwards (meeting-notes).

skills.name: Demand Forecast
skills.description: Forecast how much of each product will sell in the coming weeks or months from the sales history — trend, seasonality, promotions and stock-outs accounted for — with a range, not a single number, and the accuracy of the method on past data shown. Use when the user says "forecast demand", "how much will we sell", "sales forecast", "plan next quarter's volumes", "seasonality", "predict orders". Not for deciding what to reorder (reorder-plan) or general data exploration (explore-dataset).

skills.name: Reorder Plan
skills.description: Decide what to reorder, how much and when — from current stock, open orders, the demand forecast, each supplier's lead time and minimum order — with reorder points and safety stock per product, the products at risk of running out, excess stock tying up cash, and purchase orders drafted for the person's yes. Use when the user says "what should I reorder", "are we running out", "reorder points", "safety stock", "draft purchase orders", "overstock", "inventory planning". Not for the forecast itself (demand-forecast).

skills.name: Policy Handbook
skills.description: Build and keep the company's people handbook — time off, working hours and remote work, expenses and travel, equipment, benefits, conduct, how to raise a concern — from the policies and practices the business already has, one short section per topic, each with its source and the date it was approved, and answer employees' questions from it. Use when the user says "employee handbook", "HR policies", "write our time-off policy", "what is our policy on", "people handbook", "update the remote work policy". Not for handling a specific employee request (employee-requests) or for anything that needs an employment lawyer.

skills.name: Employee Requests
skills.description: Handle the everyday requests and questions employees bring to people ops — time off and its balance, a certificate or letter, a change of personal details, an expense or equipment question, "who do I ask about" — by applying the approved handbook, keeping a register of requests and balances, drafting the reply or the letter for the person's yes, and escalating what is sensitive. Use when the user says "log this time-off request", "how many days does X have left", "write an employment certificate", "an employee asked", "people requests", "leave tracker". Not for writing the policy itself (policy-handbook).
